# Unit 2: Mental health, mental hygiene, defence mechanisms, frustration and conflict

This notes file covers INC Unit III (5 hours). It is one of the most examined units: the mentally healthy person, defence mechanisms, and frustration and conflict appear again and again as essay and short-answer questions.

## 2.1 Concept of mental health

**Mental health** is a state of wellbeing in which a person realises his or her own abilities, can cope with the normal stresses of life, can work productively and is able to contribute to the community. This is the idea behind the World Health Organization's description; learn it in your own words.

Points to stress in an answer:

- Mental health is **more than the absence of mental illness**. A person with no diagnosis may still be unhappy and unable to cope.
- It is a **continuum**, not two boxes. Everyone moves along it.

```text
Mental health continuum
Flourishing ── Coping ── Struggling (stress, worry) ── Mental illness
   (well)                                                (needs treatment)
```

- It includes the **emotional** (feelings), **psychological** (thinking, self-image) and **social** (relationships) sides of a person.
- It is affected by biological factors (genes, brain chemistry, physical illness), psychological factors (early experiences, coping style) and social factors (poverty, family conflict, discrimination, support).

## 2.2 Mental hygiene

**Mental hygiene** is the science and practice of **preserving mental health and preventing mental illness**. Just as physical hygiene keeps the body clean and healthy, mental hygiene keeps the mind healthy.

Aims of mental hygiene:

1. **Preservative:** keep healthy people healthy (good upbringing, education, recreation).
2. **Preventive:** prevent mental illness by reducing risk factors and detecting problems early.
3. **Curative/remedial:** early treatment and rehabilitation of those who become ill.

Mental hygiene works at every level: the individual, the home, the school, the workplace and the community.

## 2.3 Characteristics of a mentally healthy person

Learn at least ten, with a one-line explanation each.

| Characteristic | What it looks like |
| --- | --- |
| Self-acceptance and self-esteem | Knows own strengths and limits; does not feel worthless |
| Realistic perception of reality | Sees situations as they are, not distorted by fear or wishful thinking |
| Emotional balance | Feels emotions but controls their expression; not easily upset |
| Ability to cope with stress | Faces problems instead of running away from them |
| Good interpersonal relationships | Can give and receive love, trust and respect |
| Independence with healthy dependence | Takes own decisions but can ask for help |
| Sense of responsibility | Accepts consequences of own actions |
| Productive work | Uses abilities, finds satisfaction in work |
| Adaptability (flexibility) | Adjusts to change — new job, illness, loss |
| Purpose and direction in life | Has goals and values |
| Integrated personality | Thoughts, feelings and actions fit together |
| Sense of humour | Can laugh, including at self |
| Social interest | Concern for others and community |
| Tolerance of frustration | Can wait, accept delay and failure |

## 2.4 Warning signs of poor mental health

Changes from the person's **usual** behaviour that last for some weeks are the clue.

- Persistent sadness, hopelessness, crying spells.
- Excessive worry, fear or restlessness.
- Marked change in sleep (too little or too much) or appetite.
- Withdrawal from friends, family and activities once enjoyed.
- Fall in work or school performance; poor concentration.
- Extreme mood swings; irritability, anger outbursts.
- Unusual beliefs or hearing/seeing things others do not.
- Increased use of alcohol, tobacco or other substances.
- Many physical complaints with no clear cause.
- Neglect of personal hygiene.
- Talk of death, being a burden, or self-harm.

**Nursing point:** any talk of suicide or self-harm is taken seriously, the person is not left alone, and it is reported at once to the senior nurse or doctor.

## 2.5 Promotive and preventive mental health strategies and services

### Levels of prevention

| Level | Aim | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Promotion | Build mental wellbeing in everyone | Life-skills education, good parenting, yoga, sports, safe workplaces |
| Primary prevention | Stop illness occurring | Antenatal care (prevent birth injury), reduce substance use, school counselling, stress management |
| Secondary prevention | Early detection and prompt treatment | Screening, crisis intervention, early referral |
| Tertiary prevention | Reduce disability; rehabilitation | Vocational training, day care, family support, prevent relapse |

### Strategies at different levels

- **Individual:** balanced diet, exercise, sleep, hobbies, relaxation, meaningful relationships, avoiding alcohol and drugs.
- **Family:** warm, consistent parenting; open communication; avoiding violence.
- **School:** life-skills, anti-bullying policies, counselling, recognising learning difficulties.
- **Workplace:** reasonable workload, support, recognition, employee assistance.
- **Community:** awareness programmes, reducing stigma, self-help groups, support for vulnerable groups.

### Services in India (check current details on the MoHFW / DGHS site)

- **National Mental Health Programme (NMHP)**, started in 1982, to make basic mental health care available to all, especially the poor, and to integrate it with general health care.
- **District Mental Health Programme (DMHP)**, added in 1996, brings community-based services to the district level: outpatient and inpatient care, outreach, awareness, training of general health staff.
- **Tele-MANAS**, the national tele-mental-health service started in October 2022, gives free round-the-clock counselling by phone; the helpline number is **14416**.
- **Mental Healthcare Act, 2017** — a rights-based law that protects the dignity of persons with mental illness, gives the right to access mental health care, and allows an advance directive. Read the current Act for details before quoting sections.
- Mental hospitals and institutes, psychiatry departments of general hospitals, counselling centres, de-addiction centres, NGOs and self-help groups.

## 2.6 Defence mechanisms

**Defence mechanisms** (ego defence or mental mechanisms) are mostly **unconscious** mental processes that protect a person from anxiety, guilt or loss of self-esteem. The idea comes from Sigmund Freud and was developed by Anna Freud.

Key points:

- Everyone uses them; they are **normal** in moderate amounts.
- They **distort or deny reality** to some extent and do not solve the real problem.
- Used **too much or rigidly**, they become unhealthy and can be part of mental illness.

| Mechanism | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Repression | Pushing painful thoughts or memories into the unconscious (involuntary) | Cannot recall details of a traumatic accident |
| Suppression | Consciously putting a worry aside (voluntary; healthy) | A nurse decides not to think about a family problem while on duty |
| Denial | Refusing to accept a painful reality | A patient told of cancer says, "The report must be wrong" |
| Projection | Blaming others for one's own unacceptable feelings | A student who did not study says the teacher hates him |
| Rationalisation | Giving a logical-sounding excuse for behaviour | "I failed because the paper was out of syllabus" |
| Displacement | Transferring feelings to a safer target | Angry with the doctor, the patient shouts at the nurse |
| Regression | Returning to behaviour of an earlier stage | A toilet-trained 4-year-old wets the bed in hospital |
| Reaction formation | Showing the opposite of the real feeling | Being extra polite to a disliked colleague |
| Sublimation | Channelling unacceptable drives into socially useful activity (healthy) | Aggression channelled into sport |
| Compensation | Making up for a weakness by excelling in another area | A student weak in sports works hard to top the class |
| Identification | Taking on the qualities of an admired person | A student nurse copies a respected senior |
| Introjection | Taking in the values of others as one's own | Child adopting parents' rules |
| Fantasy (daydreaming) | Satisfying wishes in imagination | Imagining being a famous doctor |
| Conversion | Anxiety turned into a physical symptom without a physical cause | Sudden loss of voice before a feared exam |
| Undoing | Doing something to cancel a guilty act | Bringing gifts after shouting at a child |
| Isolation of affect | Separating a feeling from a memory | Describing a relative's death without emotion |
| Intellectualisation | Using reasoning to avoid feeling | A patient talks only about statistics of the disease |
| Symbolisation | An object or act stands for a hidden idea | Repeated hand-washing standing for guilt |
| Substitution | Replacing an unreachable goal with a reachable one | Not getting MBBS, joins nursing |
| Withdrawal | Avoiding situations that cause anxiety | Staying alone in the room |

### Implications for nursing

- Recognise the mechanism; it is a **sign of anxiety**, not stubbornness or bad character.
- **Do not attack or tear down** a defence suddenly (for example arguing with a patient in denial); it may increase anxiety.
- Give time, accept the person, listen, and gently help them face reality step by step.
- **Encourage healthy mechanisms** (suppression, sublimation, compensation) and discourage harmful ones (excessive denial, projection).
- Check your own defences: a nurse who displaces anger on patients or rationalises poor care needs self-awareness.

## 2.7 Frustration

**Frustration** is the feeling of tension, disappointment and irritation when a person is blocked from reaching a goal or satisfying a need.

```text
Need/motive → Goal-directed behaviour → BARRIER → Frustration
                                                     ↓
                     Reactions: aggression, withdrawal, regression,
                     apathy, anxiety, defence mechanisms – or new solution
```

### Sources (causes) of frustration

| Source | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Environmental (external) – physical | Floods, traffic, illness, lack of money |
| Environmental – social | Rules, discrimination, family restrictions |
| Personal (internal) | Lack of ability, physical disability, unrealistic goals, low confidence |
| Conflict | Two opposing motives at the same time (see below) |

### Reactions to frustration

- **Direct approach:** more effort, a new method, changing the goal — healthy.
- **Aggression:** direct (hitting, shouting) or displaced on someone else.
- **Withdrawal or apathy:** giving up, "learned helplessness".
- **Regression, fixation:** childish or repetitive behaviour.
- **Psychosomatic symptoms:** headache, acidity.
- **Excessive use of defence mechanisms.**

## 2.8 Conflict and its types

**Conflict** is a state in which a person faces two or more opposing motives, needs or goals at the same time and must choose. Kurt Lewin described the basic types.

| Type | Choice | Example | Usual result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Approach–approach | Between two attractive goals | Two good job offers | Easiest to solve; mild stress |
| Avoidance–avoidance | Between two unpleasant choices | Painful surgery or continuing pain | Hard; person may delay, "leave the field" |
| Approach–avoidance | One goal has both attractive and unattractive sides | Wants sweets but fears gaining weight | Vacillation; anxiety |
| Double (multiple) approach–avoidance | Two or more goals, each with good and bad sides | Job in a city (good pay, away from family) vs village (less pay, near family) | Most common in real life; most stressful |

### Measures to overcome frustration and conflict

1. Identify the real problem and the needs behind it.
2. Set realistic goals that match abilities.
3. Gather information; list options, pros and cons; choose and act.
4. Accept what cannot be changed; change what can.
5. Talk to a trusted person, counsellor or teacher.
6. Use relaxation, exercise, hobbies to reduce tension.
7. Develop frustration tolerance and patience.
8. Learn from failure instead of blaming self or others.
9. Seek professional help if distress persists.

## 2.9 Role of the nurse in reducing frustration and conflict and enhancing coping

Patients are frustrated by pain, loss of independence, hospital rules, waiting, uncertainty and cost. Many face conflicts such as "surgery or no surgery", "hospital or home".

- **Assess** the source of frustration: pain, fear, unmet basic needs, poor information.
- **Meet basic needs promptly** — comfort, pain relief as ordered, food, sleep, privacy.
- **Explain procedures and rules** in simple language; uncertainty is a major frustration.
- **Allow choices** wherever possible (timing of bath, food preferences) to restore a sense of control.
- **Listen** and allow expression of feelings; accept anger without retaliating.
- **Help in decision-making** in conflicts: give information, discuss options; the decision belongs to the patient.
- **Involve the family** and support systems.
- **Teach coping skills:** relaxation breathing, problem-solving, positive self-talk.
- **Set achievable goals** in rehabilitation, praise progress.
- **Refer** to counsellor, psychologist or psychiatrist when needed.
- **Look after own stress** so that the nurse is not frustrated with patients.

**Coping** is the effort a person makes to manage stress. Problem-focused coping changes the situation; emotion-focused coping manages the feelings (more in Unit 7).

## 2.10 Dealing with ego

In Freud's structure of personality the **ego** is the realistic part of the mind that balances the demands of the **id** (instinctive wants) and the **superego** (conscience, moral rules). In everyday language "ego" also means pride or self-importance. Both meanings matter in nursing.

- **Healthy ego:** strong enough to face reality, delay gratification, solve problems, and accept criticism.
- **Ego problems:** a weak ego (easily hurt, defensive, dependent) or an inflated ego (arrogant, cannot accept mistakes or advice).

Dealing with ego in self and others:

1. **Self-awareness:** notice when hurt pride is driving your reaction.
2. **Accept feedback** as information, not as attack; separate the act from the person.
3. **Admit mistakes** early — essential for patient safety.
4. **Respect others' self-esteem:** correct in private, praise in public; never humiliate a patient.
5. **Avoid power struggles** with patients or colleagues; focus on the goal (the patient's wellbeing).
6. **Assertiveness, not aggression:** state needs clearly and politely.
7. **Humility and teamwork:** value every member of the team.

## Remember

- Mental health = wellbeing, coping, productivity, contribution; not just absence of illness; a continuum.
- Mental hygiene = preserve mental health, prevent illness, early treatment.
- Defence mechanisms are mostly unconscious, protect against anxiety, normal in moderation; suppression and sublimation are healthy.
- Do not break a patient's defence suddenly; reduce anxiety first.
- Frustration = blocked goal; conflict = opposing goals (approach–approach, avoidance–avoidance, approach–avoidance, double approach–avoidance).
- NMHP 1982, DMHP 1996, Tele-MANAS 14416, Mental Healthcare Act 2017.
- Ego = realistic mediator between id and superego; nurses accept feedback and protect patients' self-esteem.

# Unit 3: Developmental psychology and vulnerable groups

This notes file covers INC Unit IV (7 hours): development across the life span, the nurse's role in supporting normal development, psychological needs of each age group in health and sickness, an introduction to child psychology, and the psychology of vulnerable individuals.

## 3.1 Growth and development: basic ideas

- **Growth** = increase in size (height, weight); it is quantitative and measurable.
- **Development** = increase in skill and complexity of function (walking, speech, reasoning); it is qualitative.
- **Developmental psychology** studies how people change physically, cognitively, emotionally and socially from conception to death.

### Principles of development

1. Development is **continuous** — it goes on throughout life.
2. It follows a **predictable sequence** (sit before stand, babble before words).
3. **Cephalocaudal** direction: head to tail (head control before walking).
4. **Proximodistal** direction: centre to periphery (arm movements before finger skills).
5. **General to specific:** whole-body movements before precise ones.
6. Each person develops at their **own rate** (individual differences).
7. It is the result of **heredity and environment** together.
8. There are **critical (sensitive) periods** when certain skills develop best (language in early childhood).
9. All areas of development are **interrelated**: a sick child may lag in social and cognitive development too.

## 3.2 Theories you should name in answers

**Erikson's psychosocial stages** — each stage has a "crisis" to resolve.

| Age | Crisis | Successful outcome (virtue) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Infancy (0–1 yr) | Trust vs mistrust | Hope |
| Toddler (1–3 yr) | Autonomy vs shame and doubt | Will |
| Preschool (3–6 yr) | Initiative vs guilt | Purpose |
| School age (6–12 yr) | Industry vs inferiority | Competence |
| Adolescence (12–18 yr) | Identity vs role confusion | Fidelity |
| Young adult | Intimacy vs isolation | Love |
| Middle adult | Generativity vs stagnation | Care |
| Older adult | Integrity vs despair | Wisdom |

**Piaget's stages of cognitive development:**

| Stage | Age (approx.) | Key features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sensorimotor | 0–2 yr | Learns through senses and movement; object permanence develops |
| Preoperational | 2–7 yr | Symbols and language; egocentric; magical thinking; no conservation |
| Concrete operational | 7–11 yr | Logical thinking about real objects; conservation; classification |
| Formal operational | 11 yr onwards | Abstract and hypothetical thinking |

**Freud's psychosexual stages** (oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital) are also asked occasionally as a short note.

## 3.3 Development across the life span

### Prenatal period (conception to birth)

- Physical: germinal, embryonic and fetal stages; organs form in the first trimester, which is the most sensitive time.
- Influences: mother's nutrition, infections, smoking, alcohol, some medicines, radiation, maternal stress, age.
- Psychological point: mother's emotional state and acceptance of the pregnancy matter.

### Infancy and early childhood (birth to about 6 years)

- **Physical:** rapid growth; motor milestones — social smile, head control, sitting, crawling, standing, walking, running.
- **Cognitive:** sensorimotor then preoperational; first words around one year, short sentences by two to three years; curiosity, "why" questions.
- **Psychosocial:** attachment to mother or main caregiver (bonding); stranger anxiety and separation anxiety; autonomy (toilet training, "no"); play moves from solitary to parallel to cooperative; initiative in preschool years.

### Middle and late childhood (6 years to puberty)

- **Physical:** slower, steady growth; fine motor skills (writing).
- **Cognitive:** concrete operational thinking; school learning; memory improves.
- **Psychosocial:** peers become important; industry (achievement) vs inferiority; rules and fairness; gender role learning.

### Adolescence (about 12 to 18 years)

- **Physical:** puberty — growth spurt, secondary sexual characters, menarche in girls; body image concerns.
- **Cognitive:** abstract thinking, idealism; "personal fable" (feeling unique, invulnerable) leads to risk-taking.
- **Psychosocial:** search for identity; peer pressure; wish for independence; mood swings; career choices; risk of substance use, eating problems, depression.

### Early and middle adulthood (about 18 to 60 years)

- **Physical:** peak physical ability in early adulthood; gradual decline later; menopause in women around the late forties to early fifties.
- **Cognitive:** practical problem-solving and expertise grow.
- **Psychosocial:** career, marriage, parenthood (intimacy); in middle age generativity — guiding the next generation, caring for both children and ageing parents ("sandwich generation"); possible mid-life review of achievements.

### Late adulthood (about 60 years onwards)

- **Physical:** reduced sensory acuity (vision, hearing), slower reactions, chronic illnesses, reduced mobility.
- **Cognitive:** slower processing and recall of new information, but knowledge and wisdom remain; dementia is a disease, **not** normal ageing.
- **Psychosocial:** retirement, loss of spouse and friends, dependence, loneliness; integrity vs despair — looking back on life with satisfaction or regret.

### Death and dying

Elisabeth Kübler-Ross described five stages that dying people (and the bereaved) may pass through. They do not always occur in order, and people may move back and forth.

| Stage | Typical words | Nursing response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Denial | "Not me, it can't be true." | Accept; do not force the truth; stay available |
| Anger | "Why me?" | Do not take it personally; allow expression |
| Bargaining | "If I recover, I will…" | Listen; support spiritual needs |
| Depression | Sadness, withdrawal | Sit with the person; allow grief; touch, presence |
| Acceptance | Calm, peaceful | Support wishes, dignity, family time |

Understanding of death also develops with age: young children see it as temporary, by about 9–10 years most understand it is permanent and universal.

## 3.4 Role of the nurse in supporting normal growth and development

1. **Assess** development at every contact using milestones and growth charts; identify delays early and refer.
2. **Promote health:** antenatal care, breastfeeding, nutrition, immunisation, safety, hygiene.
3. **Educate parents** on stimulation, play, toilet training, discipline without harshness, and expected behaviour at each age.
4. **Support attachment:** early skin-to-skin contact, rooming-in, involve parents in care of sick children.
5. **Adapt care to the stage:** explain in age-appropriate language; allow choices; respect privacy of adolescents.
6. **Adolescent health:** counselling on puberty, nutrition, substance use, safe relationships, mental health.
7. **Adult health:** stress management, screening, work–life balance.
8. **Older adults:** prevent falls, maintain independence, social engagement, early recognition of memory problems.
9. **End of life:** comfort, dignity, honest communication, bereavement support for the family.

## 3.5 Psychological needs of various age groups in health and sickness

| Age group | Needs in health | Effect of illness / hospital | Nursing approach |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Infant | Love, security, consistent caregiver, feeding, touch | Separation distress, disturbed trust | Mother to stay; same nurse; cuddle, comfort; routine as at home |
| Toddler / preschool | Autonomy, play, routine, parental presence | Separation anxiety (protest, despair, detachment), fear of injury, regression, sees illness as punishment | Parents stay; favourite toy; simple honest explanations; play; allow small choices |
| School-age child | Achievement, peers, information, privacy | Fear of missing school, loss of control, fear of body injury | Explain using diagrams; schoolwork; contact with friends; involve in own care |
| Adolescent | Identity, independence, privacy, peer acceptance, body image | Worry about appearance, loss of independence, embarrassment | Privacy; talk directly with them; keep confidentiality where safe; peer contact |
| Adult | Work, family role, financial security, self-esteem | Worry about job, money, family; role change; anger, depression | Information; involve in decisions; social work help; family support |
| Older adult | Respect, dignity, independence, companionship, security | Confusion in new places, fear of dependence and death, loneliness | Address respectfully; orient; aids (glasses, hearing aid); unhurried care; family visits |

## 3.6 Introduction to child psychology and the nurse's role

**Child psychology** studies the behaviour, thinking and emotions of children from birth to adolescence.

Important ideas:

- **Attachment** (Bowlby): a secure bond with a caregiver is the base for later confidence and relationships.
- **Play** is the child's work and language: physical, social, intellectual and emotional development happen through play. **Therapeutic play** in hospital lets children act out fears (for example giving an injection to a doll).
- **Separation anxiety in hospital** has three phases: protest (crying, clinging), despair (quiet, sad, withdrawn), detachment (seems to accept strangers but has emotionally withdrawn). It is reduced by keeping parents with the child.
- Common **behaviour problems:** temper tantrums, thumb-sucking, bed-wetting, nail-biting, fears, school refusal, lying. Most are part of development or a reaction to stress; harsh punishment worsens them.
- **Discipline:** consistent rules, praise for good behaviour, calm consequences; avoid physical punishment.

**Nurse's role in meeting children's psychological needs:**

- Prepare the child for procedures with honest, simple words, just before the event for young children.
- Never threaten ("If you cry I'll give you an injection").
- Use distraction, toys, stories, music during painful procedures.
- Keep routines (sleep, meals) close to home routine.
- Praise cooperation; give stickers or small rewards.
- Provide a play corner; allow parents to participate in care.
- Watch for signs of abuse or neglect and report as per hospital policy and law.

## 3.7 Psychology of vulnerable individuals

**Vulnerable individuals** are people at higher risk of harm, neglect or poor health because of their physical, mental, social or economic situation.

| Group | Psychological concerns |
| --- | --- |
| Persons with disabilities (physically or mentally challenged) | Low self-esteem, dependence, social stigma, frustration, isolation; family burden |
| Women | Role overload (home and work), gender discrimination, domestic violence, stress of pregnancy and childbirth, postnatal low mood, menopause |
| The sick, especially chronically ill | Anxiety, depression, loss of role, fear of death, financial worry |
| Older adults | Loneliness, neglect, abuse, dependence |
| Children, especially orphans and street children | Insecurity, exploitation, abuse |
| Persons with mental illness | Stigma, discrimination, rejection |
| Poor, homeless, migrants, refugees | Insecurity, poor access to care |
| Persons with HIV, leprosy, TB | Stigma, fear of rejection |
| Victims of disasters, violence, abuse | Fear, trauma, grief |

## 3.8 Role of the nurse with vulnerable groups

1. **Respect and dignity:** treat every person equally, use their name, avoid labels.
2. **Non-judgemental attitude:** accept the person; avoid blaming.
3. **Assess needs** — physical, psychological, social, economic — and risks (abuse, suicide).
4. **Empower:** encourage independence, teach self-care, use aids and appliances.
5. **Advocacy:** speak up for their rights; ensure informed consent and privacy.
6. **Link with services:** social welfare schemes, disability certificates, women's helplines, shelters, NGOs, rehabilitation (check current schemes with the local health or social welfare office).
7. **Family support and education.**
8. **Fight stigma** through community awareness.
9. **Safeguarding:** recognise and report abuse or violence as per law and hospital policy.

## Remember

- Growth = size; development = function; development is sequential, cephalocaudal, proximodistal.
- Erikson: trust, autonomy, initiative, industry, identity, intimacy, generativity, integrity.
- Piaget: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational.
- Separation anxiety in hospital: protest → despair → detachment; keep parents with the child.
- Kübler-Ross: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance.
- Vulnerable groups need respect, advocacy, empowerment and links to services.

# Unit 4: Personality and psychological assessment

This notes file joins INC Unit V (Personality, 4 hours) and INC Unit VIII (Psychological assessment and tests, 4 hours). Personality is measured with psychological tests, so the two fit together. Psychometric assessment of cognitive processes (Unit VI) and of emotions and attitudes (Unit VII) is introduced in Units 6 and 7 and builds on section 4.7 here.

## 4.1 Meaning and definition of personality

The word comes from the Latin *persona*, the mask an actor wore on stage to show the character he played. In everyday speech "personality" means charm or appearance; in psychology it means much more.

**Definition (in plain words):** personality is the unique and fairly stable pattern of thinking, feeling and behaving that makes a person different from others and shapes how he or she adjusts to the environment. Gordon Allport described it as the dynamic organisation within the individual of the psychophysical systems that determine his unique adjustment to the environment — learn the key words: *dynamic*, *organisation*, *psychophysical*, *unique*, *adjustment*.

### Characteristics of personality

- **Unique:** no two people are exactly alike.
- **Consistent:** a person behaves in a similar way in similar situations.
- **Dynamic:** it grows and changes with experience.
- **Integrated:** body, mind and behaviour work as a whole.
- **Both inherited and learned.**
- **Goal-directed and adjustive.**
- **Measurable** to some extent through tests.

### Determinants of personality

| Factor | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Biological | Heredity, physique, nervous system, endocrine glands (thyroid, adrenal), health |
| Psychological | Intelligence, emotions, motives, self-concept |
| Family | Parenting style, birth order, relationships, home atmosphere |
| Social | School, peers, community, mass media |
| Cultural | Values, religion, customs, gender roles |
| Life experiences | Success, failure, trauma, illness |

## 4.2 Structure of personality (Freud)

```text
         Conscious       ┐
   ───── Preconscious ── ├─ levels of mind ("iceberg")
         Unconscious     ┘  (largest part, hidden)

   ID      – inborn drives, pleasure principle, "I want it now"
   EGO     – reality principle, balances id and superego, "let's be realistic"
   SUPEREGO– conscience and ideals, "you must not"
```

A healthy personality has a strong ego that satisfies needs in socially acceptable ways. When the ego cannot balance the demands, anxiety results and defence mechanisms are used (Unit 2).

## 4.3 Classification of personality

### Type approaches (place people into categories)

| Classifier | Types | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hippocrates (based on body fluids) | Sanguine, choleric, melancholic, phlegmatic | Cheerful and active; quick-tempered; sad and gloomy; calm and slow |
| Kretschmer (body build) | Pyknic, athletic, asthenic (leptosomic), dysplastic | Short and round – sociable, moody; muscular – energetic; thin and tall – shy, reserved; mixed |
| Sheldon (somatotypes) | Endomorph, mesomorph, ectomorph | Soft, round – relaxed, loves comfort (viscerotonic); muscular – adventurous (somatotonic); thin – sensitive, private (cerebrotonic) |
| Carl Jung | Introvert, extrovert, ambivert | Inward-looking, reserved; outgoing, social; balance of both (most people) |
| Friedman and Rosenman | Type A, Type B | Competitive, impatient, hurried, hostile (linked to heart disease); relaxed, patient, easy-going |

**Limitation of type theories:** people rarely fit one box; they oversimplify.

### Trait approaches (describe how much of each quality a person has)

A **trait** is a lasting quality such as honesty, sociability or anxiety.

- **Allport:** cardinal traits (dominate a whole life, rare), central traits (5–10 main ones that describe a person), secondary traits (appear in some situations).
- **Cattell:** surface traits (visible) and source traits (underlying); 16 source traits measured by the 16PF questionnaire.
- **Eysenck:** three dimensions — extraversion–introversion, neuroticism–stability, psychoticism.
- **Big Five (five-factor model)** — remember **OCEAN**: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism.

### Other approaches (name only if asked)

- **Psychoanalytic** (Freud, Jung, Adler): unconscious forces and early experience.
- **Humanistic** (Rogers, Maslow): self-concept, growth, self-actualisation.
- **Behavioural / social learning** (Skinner, Bandura): personality is learned behaviour, through reward and imitation.

## 4.4 Measurement and evaluation of personality – introduction

| Method | Description | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Interview | Structured or unstructured conversation | Case history interview |
| Observation | Watch behaviour in natural or set situations | Behaviour in ward or play |
| Rating scales | Someone who knows the person rates traits on a scale | Teacher rates punctuality 1–5 |
| Personality inventories (questionnaires) | Many yes/no or agree/disagree items, scored against norms | MMPI, 16PF, Eysenck Personality Questionnaire |
| Projective techniques | Ambiguous stimuli; person "projects" inner feelings into the answer | Rorschach inkblot test, Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), sentence completion, word association, draw-a-person |
| Situational tests | Behaviour observed in a real-life-like task | Group discussion, stress interview |
| Biographical data / autobiography | Life history, diaries | — |

Projective tests need specially trained psychologists to score and interpret; nurses observe and report, they do not interpret these tests.

## 4.5 Alteration in personality

Personality can be altered in two broad ways.

**1. Personality disorders** — long-standing, rigid, unhelpful patterns of inner experience and behaviour that begin in adolescence or early adulthood and cause distress or problems in relationships and work. They are grouped into three clusters:

| Cluster | Description | Types |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A – odd, eccentric | Suspicious, detached, strange beliefs | Paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal |
| B – dramatic, emotional, erratic | Impulsive, attention-seeking, unstable | Antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic |
| C – anxious, fearful | Worried, dependent, perfectionist | Avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive |

**2. Personality change** from another cause:

- Brain injury or tumour, especially of the frontal lobe (disinhibition, irritability, poor judgement).
- Dementia, stroke, epilepsy.
- Long-term alcohol or drug use.
- Severe mental illness (schizophrenia, severe depression).
- Hormonal disorders (hyperthyroidism — anxious, irritable; hypothyroidism — slow, dull).
- Severe trauma, prolonged stress.

## 4.6 Role of the nurse in identifying personality and improving altered personality

**Identification**

- Observe and record behaviour objectively: how the patient relates to staff, handles frustration, follows advice.
- Take a history from the patient and family: previous personality ("what was he like before?"), recent changes.
- Report sudden personality change at once — it may mean a medical cause (head injury, infection, metabolic problem).
- Help the team with rating scales and checklists as instructed.

**Care and improvement**

- Build a consistent, trusting relationship; same nurse where possible.
- Set clear, firm but kind limits for manipulative or aggressive behaviour; apply rules consistently across staff.
- Reinforce acceptable behaviour with praise.
- Teach social skills, anger management, problem-solving.
- Encourage self-awareness and responsibility for actions.
- Involve family; teach them to respond consistently.
- Treat underlying causes (medical, substance use) and refer to mental health services.
- Understand your own reactions: some personalities provoke staff; stay professional.
- Use personality knowledge in daily care: an introvert may need privacy and written information; an extrovert may prefer group activities; a Type A patient after heart attack needs help to slow down.

## 4.7 Psychological assessment and tests – introduction

**Psychological assessment** is the collection of information about a person's behaviour, abilities, personality and emotions, using interviews, observation, history and tests, to understand the person and help decisions.

A **psychological test** is a standardised, objective measure of a sample of behaviour. "Standardised" means the same instructions, conditions and scoring for everyone, and scores are compared with **norms** (average scores of a large similar group).

### Types of psychological tests

| Basis | Types |
| --- | --- |
| What is measured | Intelligence, aptitude, achievement, personality, interest, attitude, neuropsychological |
| Number tested | Individual tests (one at a time, e.g. Wechsler scales); group tests (many at once) |
| Form | Verbal (language used); non-verbal (pictures, symbols); performance (handling objects, puzzles, block designs) |
| Time | Speed tests (easy items, strict time); power tests (items get harder, more time) |
| Scoring | Objective (fixed key); subjective (examiner judgement, e.g. projective) |
| Standardisation | Standardised vs teacher-made / informal |

### Development of a test (steps)

```text
1. Decide the purpose and what will be measured
2. Write a large pool of items
3. Try out on a small group (pilot); item analysis – keep good items
4. Final form with fixed instructions, time and scoring key
5. Standardise on a large representative group → prepare norms
6. Check reliability and validity
7. Prepare the manual
```

### Characteristics of a good test

| Characteristic | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Reliability | Gives consistent results on repeated use (test–retest, split-half, parallel forms) |
| Validity | Measures what it claims to measure (content, criterion, construct validity) |
| Objectivity | Scores do not depend on who scores it |
| Standardisation | Uniform procedure for giving and scoring |
| Norms | Reference scores of a defined group for comparison |
| Practicability (usability) | Easy to give, score and interpret; reasonable cost and time |
| Discrimination | Separates high and low performers |
| Cultural fairness | Suitable for the person's language and background |

### Principles of psychological testing

1. Only **trained and qualified** persons give and interpret tests.
2. **Informed consent**; explain the purpose.
3. **Confidentiality** of results.
4. Good **rapport**; reduce anxiety, which lowers scores.
5. Suitable **environment**: quiet, well lit, no interruptions.
6. Follow **standard instructions** exactly.
7. Choose a test suited to age, language and culture.
8. A test result is **one piece of information** — never label a person on one score.

### Uses of psychological tests

- **Clinical:** diagnosis (intellectual disability, dementia, depression), planning and evaluating treatment.
- **Educational:** identify learning difficulty, giftedness, guidance.
- **Vocational:** selection and placement, career counselling.
- **Research.**
- **Legal:** fitness to stand trial, disability assessment.
- **Self-understanding.**

### Interpretation

- A **raw score** means little alone; it is converted to a standard form — percentile rank, standard score, IQ — and compared with norms.
- Consider the person's health, mood, motivation, education and culture at the time of testing.
- Interpretation is done by a psychologist; results are discussed with the team and explained to the person sensitively.

## 4.8 Role of the nurse in psychological assessment

- **Prepare the patient:** explain the purpose, reassure, see that they have slept and eaten, and have glasses or hearing aids.
- **Arrange the setting:** quiet room, privacy, time agreed with the psychologist.
- **Observe and record** behaviour on the ward — sleep, appetite, mood, interaction — which supplements test findings.
- **Use simple screening tools** the nurse is trained in, as per hospital policy (for example orientation questions, pain scales, mood or anxiety checklists), and report findings.
- **Maintain confidentiality** of results.
- **Support the patient** after testing, especially if results are worrying.
- **Use results in care planning** — for example simpler teaching for a patient with low cognitive scores.
- **Avoid labelling** or discussing results casually.

## Remember

- Personality = unique, stable, dynamic pattern of thinking, feeling, behaving; from Latin *persona*.
- Freud: id (pleasure), ego (reality), superego (conscience).
- Types: Hippocrates, Kretschmer, Sheldon, Jung, Type A/B. Traits: Allport, Cattell (16PF), Eysenck, Big Five (OCEAN).
- Measurement: interview, observation, rating scale, inventories (MMPI, 16PF), projective (Rorschach, TAT).
- Personality disorders: clusters A (odd), B (dramatic), C (anxious).
- Good test = reliable, valid, objective, standardised, normed, practicable.
- Nurse prepares, observes, records, keeps confidentiality; psychologist interprets.

# Unit 5: Cognitive processes I – attention, perception, intelligence and aptitude

INC Unit VI (Cognitive process) is the largest unit of the course (16 hours), so it is split into two notes files. This file covers attention, perception, intelligence (with mental deficiency) and aptitude. Unit 6 covers learning, memory, thinking, psychometric assessment of cognitive processes and alterations in cognition.

**Cognition** means all the mental processes by which we take in, store, change and use information: attending, perceiving, learning, remembering, thinking, reasoning and problem-solving.

## 5.1 Attention

**Attention** is the process of focusing consciousness on one object, idea or activity while ignoring others. It works like a torch: what is in the beam is clear, the rest is dim.

### Types of attention

| Type | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Involuntary (non-volitional) | Drawn automatically by a strong stimulus, without effort | Turning at a loud crash |
| Voluntary (volitional) | Deliberately directed with effort and will | Concentrating on a lecture |
| Habitual | Voluntary attention that has become automatic through habit and interest | A mother waking at her baby's faint cry; an ICU nurse noticing a monitor alarm |
| Selective | Picking one stimulus from many | Following one conversation in a noisy ward |
| Divided | Attending to two tasks at once | Talking to the patient while checking the drip rate |
| Sustained (vigilance) | Keeping attention over a long time | Watching an anaesthesia monitor |

### Determinants (factors) of attention

**External (objective) factors — in the stimulus:**

- Intensity and size (loud sound, bright light, big headline)
- Novelty (something new)
- Change and movement (flashing light)
- Repetition (an advertisement repeated)
- Contrast (red word on white page)
- Colour, position (top-left of a page) and duration

**Internal (subjective) factors — in the person:**

- Interest and motives (a hungry person notices food smells)
- Needs and drives
- Mental set or expectation (waiting for one's name to be called)
- Emotional state and mood
- Fatigue, illness, drugs, alcohol (reduce attention)
- Past experience and training

### Span, duration and degree of attention

- **Span of attention (span of apprehension):** the number of items a person can grasp in one brief glance — usually about six to seven separate items for adults; fewer for children.
- **Duration:** attention cannot stay perfectly steady; it fluctuates every few seconds and tires with time. In a lecture, attention drops after about 15–20 minutes unless the activity changes.
- **Degree:** attention can be full and concentrated or partial and scattered, depending on interest, health and distractions.
- **Distraction:** any stimulus that pulls attention away. Shifting of attention is normal; distractibility is excessive shifting.

### Alterations in attention

| Alteration | Description | Seen in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Distractibility | Attention drawn by every trivial stimulus | Mania, delirium, anxiety |
| Inattention / poor concentration | Cannot focus | Depression, fatigue, ADHD |
| Hypervigilance | Over-alert, scanning for danger | Anxiety, PTSD, paranoia |
| Narrowing of attention | Focus only on one thing, misses others | Severe anxiety, pain |
| Clouding of consciousness | Reduced awareness | Delirium, head injury, drug effects |
| Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder | Inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity from childhood | Children, may continue into adult life |

### Nursing applications

- Health teaching: short sessions, one main point, use colour and demonstration, repeat, avoid noise.
- Pain: distraction (music, talking, play) shifts attention and reduces pain felt.
- Patient safety: reduce distraction during drug preparation (quiet zone), double-check.
- Note attention on mental state examination (ask the patient to count backwards).

## 5.2 Perception

**Perception** is the process of selecting, organising and interpreting sensations so that they have meaning. Sensation gives raw data; perception gives the meaning.

```text
Stimulus → Sensation (receptor) → Attention (selection)
        → Organisation → Interpretation (with past experience) → Meaningful percept → Response
```

Example: a nurse hears a sound (sensation), attends to it, recognises it as the pulse oximeter alarm (perception) and checks the patient (response).

### Principles of perceptual organisation (Gestalt laws)

| Principle | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Figure–ground | We see an object (figure) standing out from a background (ground) |
| Proximity | Items close together are seen as a group |
| Similarity | Similar items (shape, colour) are grouped |
| Closure | We fill gaps to see a complete figure |
| Continuity | We follow smooth, continuous lines |
| Simplicity (good form) | We see the simplest possible shape |

```text
Proximity:   ●●  ●●  ●●     → seen as three pairs
Closure:     ( _  _ )       → seen as a complete circle
```

### Perceptual constancy

We see objects as stable even when the image on the eye changes:

- **Size constancy:** a person walking away does not seem to shrink.
- **Shape constancy:** a door seen at an angle is still seen as rectangular.
- **Colour and brightness constancy:** a white sheet looks white in dim light.

**Depth perception** uses binocular cues (two eyes seeing slightly different images) and monocular cues (relative size, overlap, shading, linear perspective).

### Factors affecting perception

| Factor | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Characteristics of the stimulus | Clarity, intensity, familiarity |
| Attention and interest | We notice what interests us |
| Past experience and learning | An experienced nurse recognises subtle cyanosis |
| Motivation and needs | A thirsty person sees water everywhere |
| Mental set and expectation | Seeing what we expect to see |
| Emotions | Fear makes shadows look like threats |
| Culture | Interpretation of symptoms, gestures, colours |
| Physical state | Fever, fatigue, sensory loss, drugs, alcohol |
| Age | Children and older adults may misinterpret more |

### Errors of perception (alteration)

| Error | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Illusion | Misinterpretation of a real stimulus | A rope seen as a snake in dim light; a frightened, feverish child sees a shadow as a ghost |
| Hallucination | Perception without any external stimulus | Hearing voices when no one is speaking (schizophrenia, alcohol withdrawal, delirium) |
| Agnosia | Cannot recognise objects despite intact senses | After certain brain injuries |
| Depersonalisation / derealisation | Feeling of self or surroundings being unreal | Severe anxiety |

**Nursing role:** good lighting at night, reduce shadows and noise, orient confused patients, never argue with a hallucinating patient or pretend to share the experience — acknowledge the feeling ("I don't hear voices, but I can see you are frightened"), keep them safe and report.

## 5.3 Intelligence

### Meaning

There is no single agreed definition. In plain words, **intelligence** is the general mental ability to learn from experience, understand ideas, reason, solve problems and adjust to new situations. David Wechsler described it as the global capacity to act purposefully, think rationally and deal effectively with the environment.

### Theories (name in answers)

| Theorist | Theory |
| --- | --- |
| Charles Spearman | Two-factor theory: a general factor *g* in all tasks plus specific factors *s* for each task |
| L. L. Thurstone | Primary mental abilities: verbal meaning, word fluency, number, space, memory, perceptual speed, reasoning |
| J. P. Guilford | Structure of intellect: many abilities from operations × contents × products |
| Howard Gardner | Multiple intelligences: linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalistic |
| Robert Sternberg | Triarchic: analytical, creative, practical intelligence |
| Daniel Goleman (popularised) | Emotional intelligence: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills |

Emotional intelligence is especially useful for nurses: understanding and managing one's own feelings and responding to patients' feelings.

### Effect of heredity and environment on intelligence

- **Heredity:** twin studies show identical twins have closer intelligence scores than fraternal twins, even when reared apart; genetic conditions such as Down syndrome lower intelligence.
- **Environment:** nutrition (iodine, iron, protein), prenatal care, birth complications, stimulating home, schooling, poverty, language, culture, and emotional security all affect intelligence. Children moved from deprived to enriched homes show gains.
- **Conclusion:** heredity sets the upper and lower limits; environment decides where within these limits a person reaches. They interact; it is not "either–or".

### Measurement of intelligence – introduction

- **Alfred Binet** and Théodore Simon prepared the first practical intelligence test (1905) in France to identify children needing extra help in school. The idea of **mental age (MA)** came from this work.
- Lewis Terman revised it as the **Stanford–Binet** test and used the **intelligence quotient**:

```text
IQ = (Mental age ÷ Chronological age) × 100
Example: a 10-year-old who performs like an average 12-year-old
IQ = (12 ÷ 10) × 100 = 120
```

- Modern tests (Wechsler scales — WAIS for adults, WISC for children) use a **deviation IQ**: the person's score compared with others of the same age, with the average set at 100.
- Other tests: Raven's Progressive Matrices (non-verbal, culture-reduced); performance tests such as form boards; Indian tests and adaptations exist, such as Bhatia's battery of performance tests and Malin's adaptation of the Wechsler scale for Indian children.

### Classification of intelligence (commonly used IQ ranges)

| IQ | Classification |
| --- | --- |
| 130 and above | Very superior (gifted) |
| 120–129 | Superior |
| 110–119 | High average (bright normal) |
| 90–109 | Average |
| 80–89 | Low average (dull normal) |
| 70–79 | Borderline |
| Below 70 | Intellectual disability (mental deficiency) |

Ranges vary slightly between textbooks and tests; learn the pattern, with average around 90–110.

### Mental deficiency (intellectual disability)

The older term "mental deficiency" or "mental retardation" has been replaced by **intellectual disability**: significantly below-average intellectual functioning **together with** difficulty in everyday adaptive skills (self-care, communication, social skills), beginning before 18 years of age.

| Degree | Approximate IQ | Typical abilities |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mild | 50–69 | Can learn basic reading and arithmetic, many live independently with some support |
| Moderate | 35–49 | Can learn self-care and simple work under supervision |
| Severe | 20–34 | Limited speech, needs help with most activities |
| Profound | Below 20 | Needs constant care |

**Causes:** genetic (Down syndrome, fragile X), prenatal (infections such as rubella, maternal alcohol use, iodine deficiency), perinatal (birth asphyxia, prematurity), postnatal (meningitis, head injury, severe malnutrition, hypothyroidism untreated), and social deprivation.

**Prevention and nursing role:** antenatal care, iodised salt, immunisation (rubella), safe delivery, newborn screening for hypothyroidism where available, early stimulation; early identification of developmental delay; training in self-care with small steps and rewards; support and counselling of parents; inform families about special education and disability benefits (check current schemes locally); protect from abuse.

## 5.4 Aptitude

**Aptitude** is a person's natural capacity or potential to learn a particular skill quickly and do well in it with training. Intelligence is general ability; aptitude is specific potential; achievement is what has already been learned.

| Term | Looks at |
| --- | --- |
| Intelligence | General mental ability |
| Aptitude | Future potential in a specific area |
| Achievement | Present level of learning |
| Interest | Liking for an activity |

### Types of aptitude

- Verbal (language), numerical, abstract reasoning, spatial (visualising shapes), mechanical, clerical (speed and accuracy), musical, artistic, scientific, teaching, manual dexterity, social (dealing with people).

**Aptitude tests:** for one area (special aptitude tests) or several (batteries, e.g. the Differential Aptitude Tests, General Aptitude Test Battery). Nursing entrance assessments often look at reasoning, language and interpersonal aptitude.

### Individual differences and variability

- People differ from each other (**inter-individual differences**) in intelligence, aptitude, personality and interests.
- One person's abilities also differ from area to area (**intra-individual differences**) — good at language, weak in mathematics.
- Abilities are distributed in the population in a **normal (bell-shaped) curve**: most people are near the average, few at the extremes.

```text
           frequency
              ▲        ___
              │      /     \
              │    /         \
              │___/           \___
              └─────────────────────► ability
               low   average    high
```

- **Causes of individual differences:** heredity, environment, age, sex-role training, education, socio-economic status, culture, health.
- **Uses for nurses:** teach patients at their level, use strengths in rehabilitation, place staff in suitable areas, avoid comparing children harshly.

## Remember

- Attention: involuntary, voluntary, habitual; determinants external (intensity, novelty, movement, contrast) and internal (interest, need, set).
- Span of attention ≈ six to seven items; attention fluctuates and tires.
- Perception = organising and interpreting sensations; Gestalt laws; constancy; illusion (real stimulus misread) vs hallucination (no stimulus).
- IQ = MA ÷ CA × 100; average 90–110; below 70 with adaptive problems = intellectual disability.
- Binet (first test, 1905), Terman (IQ), Wechsler (deviation IQ).
- Heredity sets limits; environment decides development within them.
- Aptitude = potential in a specific area; differences follow a normal curve.

# Unit 6: Cognitive processes II – learning, memory and thinking

This notes file is the second half of INC Unit VI. It covers learning and habit formation, memory and forgetting, thinking, reasoning and problem-solving, psychometric assessment of cognitive processes, and alterations in cognitive processes.

## 6.1 Learning

**Learning** is a relatively permanent change in behaviour (or in the potential for behaviour) that results from experience or practice. Changes due to growth, fatigue, illness or drugs are not learning.

Key words in the definition: *relatively permanent*, *change in behaviour*, *experience or practice*.

### Types of learning

**1. Classical conditioning (Ivan Pavlov)**

A neutral stimulus, after being paired many times with a stimulus that naturally produces a response, comes to produce that response by itself.

```text
Before:  Food (UCS) ──────────────→ Salivation (UCR)
         Bell (neutral) ──────────→ no salivation
During:  Bell + Food, repeated ───→ Salivation
After:   Bell (CS) ───────────────→ Salivation (CR)
```

- UCS = unconditioned stimulus, UCR = unconditioned response, CS = conditioned stimulus, CR = conditioned response.
- **Extinction:** the CR fades if the CS is given repeatedly without the UCS.
- **Spontaneous recovery:** an extinguished response returns briefly after rest.
- **Generalisation:** similar stimuli also produce the response; **discrimination:** responding only to the exact stimulus.
- **Nursing example:** a child who had painful injections cries at the sight of any white coat (generalisation). Anticipatory nausea before a chemotherapy session is another conditioned response.

**2. Trial-and-error learning (Edward Thorndike)**

A hungry cat in a puzzle box makes many random movements, accidentally opens the latch, and gets food; over trials, useless movements drop and the right one comes faster. Thorndike's laws:

- **Law of readiness:** learning is better when the learner is ready.
- **Law of exercise:** practice strengthens connections; disuse weakens them.
- **Law of effect:** responses followed by satisfaction are strengthened; those followed by discomfort are weakened.

**3. Operant (instrumental) conditioning (B. F. Skinner)**

Behaviour is shaped by its consequences.

| Consequence | Effect on behaviour | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Positive reinforcement (something pleasant added) | Increases | Praise when a patient walks with the walker |
| Negative reinforcement (something unpleasant removed) | Increases | Pain goes away after the patient changes position, so he repeats it |
| Punishment (unpleasant added or pleasant removed) | Decreases | Fine for late arrival |
| Extinction (no reinforcement) | Decreases | Ignoring attention-seeking tantrums |

**Shaping** = reinforcing small steps towards the final behaviour; used in rehabilitation and in training children with intellectual disability.

**4. Insight learning (Wolfgang Köhler)**

Sudden understanding of the relationship between parts of a problem ("aha!"). Köhler's chimpanzee Sultan joined two sticks to reach a banana outside the cage. Insight learning is quick, remembered well and transferred to new problems.

**5. Observational (social) learning (Albert Bandura)**

Learning by watching others (models) and imitating them. Bandura's "Bobo doll" studies showed children copy aggressive behaviour they observe. Steps: attention → retention → reproduction → motivation. Student nurses learn many skills by watching senior nurses — so seniors must model correct practice.

### Factors influencing learning

| Learner factors | Material / method factors | Environment factors |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Age and maturation | Meaningfulness of material | Quiet, well-lit, ventilated room |
| Intelligence and aptitude | Length and difficulty | Freedom from distraction |
| Motivation and interest | Spaced vs massed practice | Teacher's attitude |
| Physical health, fatigue, sleep | Whole vs part method | Group atmosphere |
| Emotional state, anxiety | Use of senses (audiovisual aids) | Time of day |
| Previous knowledge | Feedback and reinforcement | Culture and language |

### The learning process and learning curve

```text
Motive (need) → Goal → Activity (trying) → Reinforcement → Learning → Fixation (practice)
```

- A **learning curve** plots progress against practice. It often rises quickly at first, then flattens into a **plateau** (no apparent progress for a while, due to fatigue, loss of interest or the need to combine sub-skills), then rises again with continued practice.
- **Transfer of learning:** learning in one situation helps (positive transfer) or hinders (negative transfer) learning in another. Learning aseptic technique for dressing helps in learning catheterisation (positive transfer).

### Habit formation

A **habit** is an acquired behaviour pattern that, through repetition, becomes automatic and is performed with little conscious effort.

**Forming a good habit (classic maxims, often attributed to William James):**

1. Start with a strong, clear decision and announce it.
2. Never allow an exception until the habit is firmly fixed.
3. Act on every opportunity to practise.
4. Practise regularly at the same time and place (cue).
5. Reward yourself for each success.

**Breaking a bad habit:** become aware of the cue, avoid triggers, replace with an alternative behaviour, gradual reduction or sudden stop as suitable, remove reward, get support and keep a record.

**Nursing value:** good habits (hand hygiene, checking patient identity, documentation) protect patients; health teaching aims at new habits — exercise, medication timing, tobacco cessation.

## 6.2 Memory

**Memory** is the mental ability to encode, store and later retrieve information and experiences.

### Stages of memory

```text
Encoding (registration) → Storage (retention) → Retrieval (recall/recognition)
```

### Types (stores) of memory

| Store | Capacity | Duration | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sensory memory | Large | Less than 1–2 seconds | Brief trace of what the senses received; lost unless attended |
| Short-term (working) memory | About 7 ± 2 items | About 20–30 seconds without rehearsal | Holding a phone number while dialling; improved by chunking |
| Long-term memory | Practically unlimited | Minutes to a lifetime | Needs meaningful encoding and rehearsal |

Long-term memory has kinds:

- **Explicit (declarative):** episodic (personal events — "my first injection") and semantic (facts — normal pulse rate).
- **Implicit (non-declarative):** procedural (skills — riding a bicycle, giving an injection), conditioned responses.

### Measuring memory (methods of retention)

- **Recall:** reproduce information without cues (essay answer).
- **Recognition:** identify the correct item from choices (MCQ) — easier than recall.
- **Relearning (savings) method:** time saved in learning the material again.
- **Reconstruction:** rearranging items into their original order.

### Factors influencing memory

- Attention and interest at the time of learning.
- Meaningfulness and organisation of material.
- Repetition, revision and overlearning.
- Spacing of practice; sleep after learning.
- Emotional state: mild arousal helps, severe anxiety hinders.
- Health: fatigue, illness, alcohol, some drugs, head injury and ageing reduce memory.
- Interference from similar material.

### Methods to improve memory

1. **Understand** before memorising; link new facts to what you know.
2. **Organise** in headings, tables, flow charts.
3. **Chunking:** group items (a 10-digit number in 3–3–4 groups).
4. **Mnemonics:** acronyms (OCEAN for Big Five), rhymes, visual images.
5. **Spaced revision** rather than cramming; revise within a day, a week, a month.
6. **Recitation / self-testing:** close the book and recall.
7. **Overlearning:** practise beyond the first correct recall.
8. **Use many senses:** read, write, speak, draw.
9. **Whole method** for short meaningful material, **part method** for long material.
10. **Sleep, exercise, nutrition** and avoiding stress.

**Teaching patients:** older or anxious patients remember little of what is said in a busy clinic, so give one or two key points, repeat, give written or picture instructions, ask them to repeat back ("teach-back"), and involve the family.

### Forgetting

**Forgetting** is the loss or inability to retrieve information that was once learned. Hermann Ebbinghaus showed that forgetting is fastest soon after learning and then slows (the **curve of forgetting**) — the reason for early revision.

```text
Retention
100% ●
     │ \
     │  \
     │    \___
     │        ‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾────── 
     └──────────────────────► time (hours → days)
```

**Causes (theories) of forgetting:**

| Theory | Explanation |
| --- | --- |
| Decay (disuse) | Memory traces fade if not used |
| Interference – proactive | Old learning interferes with new (old phone number blocks new one) |
| Interference – retroactive | New learning interferes with old |
| Retrieval failure | Information is stored but cannot be accessed without the right cue ("tip of the tongue") |
| Motivated forgetting / repression | Painful memories pushed out of awareness |
| Organic causes | Brain injury, dementia, alcohol, ECT, ageing |

Forgetting is not always bad: it clears unnecessary detail and painful experiences.

## 6.3 Thinking

**Thinking** is the mental manipulation of information — images, symbols, concepts and language — to understand, decide, plan and solve problems. It is "behaviour carried on inside the mind".

### Elements (tools) of thinking

Images, concepts, symbols and signs, language, and propositions (statements).

### Types of thinking

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Perceptual (concrete) thinking | Based on objects present; seen in young children |
| Conceptual (abstract) thinking | Using ideas and concepts not physically present |
| Reflective thinking | Careful, logical thinking to solve a problem |
| Creative thinking | Producing new and original ideas |
| Critical thinking | Questioning, analysing evidence, judging before accepting — essential in nursing |
| Convergent thinking | Arriving at one correct answer |
| Divergent thinking | Producing many possible answers (creativity) |
| Autistic (fantasy) thinking | Daydreaming, wish-fulfilling, not reality-based |

### Levels of thinking

Thinking develops from the **perceptual** level (things present) to the **conceptual** level (ideas and classes) to the **abstract or symbolic** level (principles, hypotheses) — matching Piaget's stages.

### Reasoning

- **Inductive reasoning:** from specific observations to a general rule ("Several patients with these signs had dengue; this pattern suggests dengue").
- **Deductive reasoning:** from a general rule to a specific case ("All patients on bed rest are at risk of pressure sores; Mr A is on bed rest; so Mr A is at risk").

### Problem-solving

Steps:

1. Identify and define the problem.
2. Collect information.
3. Form possible solutions (hypotheses).
4. Evaluate and choose the best.
5. Act.
6. Evaluate the result and modify if needed.

These steps are the same as the **nursing process**: assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation and evaluation.

**Strategies:** trial and error, algorithms (step-by-step rules that always work, such as a protocol), heuristics (rules of thumb, quick but may err), insight.

**Barriers:** mental set (sticking to one approach), functional fixedness (seeing objects only in their usual use), lack of information, emotional stress, fatigue, bias.

## 6.4 Psychometric assessment of cognitive processes – introduction

Tests that measure cognitive functions:

| Function | Examples of tools |
| --- | --- |
| Overall cognition (screening) | Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), clock-drawing test, bedside orientation questions |
| Intelligence | Wechsler scales, Stanford–Binet, Raven's matrices, Indian adaptations |
| Memory | Wechsler Memory Scale; Indian memory scales such as the PGI Memory Scale |
| Attention and concentration | Digit span, serial subtraction (100 − 7), letter cancellation tests |
| Aptitude | Differential Aptitude Tests |
| Neuropsychological | Batteries testing language, planning, visuo-spatial ability after brain injury |

Screening tests are quick and can be used by trained nurses; detailed tests are given and interpreted by psychologists.

**Simple bedside cognitive assessment by a nurse:** orientation to time, place and person; attention (spell a word backwards, serial sevens); immediate and delayed recall of three words; simple commands; judgement ("What would you do if you smelt smoke?").

## 6.5 Alterations in cognitive processes

| Process | Alteration | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Consciousness / orientation | Disorientation; clouding; delirium (acute, fluctuating confusion) | Post-operative older adult, high fever, infection |
| Attention | Distractibility, poor concentration | Anxiety, mania |
| Perception | Illusions, hallucinations | Delirium, schizophrenia, alcohol withdrawal |
| Memory | Amnesia — anterograde (cannot form new memories after an event) and retrograde (loss of memories before it); confabulation (filling gaps with made-up stories) | Head injury; alcohol-related memory disorder |
| Thinking – form and stream | Flight of ideas, thought block, poverty of thought, perseveration | Mania, schizophrenia, dementia |
| Thinking – content | Delusions (fixed false beliefs not shared by culture), obsessions (unwanted repeated thoughts) | Psychosis, obsessive-compulsive disorder |
| Intelligence | Intellectual disability (from childhood); dementia (acquired decline in adults) | Down syndrome; Alzheimer's disease |
| Judgement and insight | Poor judgement, lack of insight into illness | Severe mental illness, frontal lobe damage |

### Nursing role in altered cognition

- Assess and record orientation, attention and memory regularly; report sudden change (delirium is a medical emergency).
- Reorient: clocks, calendars, name boards, family photos, introduce yourself each time.
- Keep a safe environment: bed rails as per policy, night light, remove hazards, supervision.
- Simple, short instructions, one at a time; give time to respond.
- Routine and the same caregivers reduce confusion.
- Memory aids: lists, pill organisers, alarms.
- Do not argue with delusions; do not agree with them either; focus on feelings and reality.
- Support and teach the family.

## Remember

- Learning = relatively permanent change in behaviour through experience.
- Pavlov (classical), Thorndike (trial and error; laws of readiness, exercise, effect), Skinner (operant; reinforcement), Köhler (insight), Bandura (observation).
- Plateau = flat part of the learning curve; transfer of learning positive or negative.
- Memory: encoding → storage → retrieval; STM about 7 ± 2 items, about 20–30 seconds.
- Ebbinghaus: forgetting is fastest soon after learning — revise early and spaced.
- Interference: proactive (old blocks new), retroactive (new blocks old).
- Problem-solving steps = nursing process.
- Delirium (acute, fluctuating) vs dementia (gradual, progressive).
